opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and it's one of the things that initially made people skeptical of the whole joint-embedding predictive approach. When you start from a randomly initialized network, both your context encoder and your target encoder are producing essentially arbitrary features. So you're asking the model to predict representations that are themselves meaningless at the start, and the obvious worry is that the easiest way to solve that prediction problem is to collapse: just map everything to a constant and the prediction loss goes to zero.

So the way I think about it is in two parts. The first is preventing collapse, and there are a few tools for that. In I-JEPA and V-JEPA we use an asymmetric architecture: the target encoder is an exponential moving average of the context encoder, there's a stop-gradient on the targets, and there's a predictor network sitting between them. That combination of asymmetry and slowly moving targets turns out, empirically, to be enough to keep the representations from collapsing, even though there's no explicit contrastive term or variance regularizer. There's also some nice theoretical work showing that, under these dynamics, the network tends to pick up the high-influence, predictive features first rather than just shrinking to a trivial solution.

The second part, which I think is the more interesting one, is what makes the representations meaningful rather than just non-collapsed. And there the key is really the design of the prediction task: the masking strategy. If you mask small, random patches, the model can solve the task with low-level interpolation, local texture and color, and you don't get semantic features. But if you mask large, spatially, or in video spatio-temporally, contiguous blocks, the model can't just copy nearby pixels. It has to reason about what's likely to be there at a more abstract level: there's an object, it has parts, it's going to move in a certain way. And because we're predicting in representation space rather than pixel space, the model is free to throw away the unpredictable details and focus on the stuff that actually is predictable.

So there's a kind of bootstrapping that happens. Early on, the targets are fairly simple features, and the model learns to predict those. As the context encoder improves, the EMA target encoder improves with it, so the targets get richer, and the prediction task gets more semantically demanding. You get this virtuous cycle where the representation and the target co-evolve.

I'd say it's still not fully understood. There's a lot of sensitivity to things like the EMA schedule, the predictor's capacity, and the masking ratio, and part of the ongoing research is making this more principled so it's less of an art and more something you can reason about ahead of time.

r001.rationale: It says the easiest way to solve the prediction problem could be to collapse the representations, indicating that the prediction objective favors simplifying them to ease prediction.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes mapping everything to a constant as a way to make the prediction loss zero.

r003.rationale: It names anti-collapse mechanisms used in I-JEPA and V-JEPA, but does not identify adapting existing self-supervised learning techniques as the approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the crux of the whole thing, right? When you're doing joint-embedding predictive architectures, you don't have a target in pixel space. The target is itself a representation, and that representation is coming from the model you're training. So on day one, when everything is randomly initialized, the target encoder is producing basically noise, and you're asking the predictor to predict noise from other noise. The obvious failure mode is collapse: the easiest way to make prediction trivial is for the encoder to just output a constant, or something close to it, and then you've "solved" the task and learned nothing.

So the way I think about it is you have two problems layered on top of each other. One is preventing collapse, and the other is actually making the learning signal informative enough that the representation gets better over time rather than just staying non-degenerate.

For the collapse piece, the thing that's worked well for us, in I-JEPA and V-JEPA, is the asymmetry between the two branches. The target encoder is an exponential moving average of the context encoder, so it moves slowly, and you don't backprop through it. That means the context encoder is always chasing a slightly stale, smoothed version of itself. People have tried to explain exactly why that avoids collapse, and there's some nice theory now around the predictor plus the EMA acting like an implicit regularizer, but empirically it's been quite robust. You could also go the explicit route, like the VICReg-style variance and covariance terms, and that's a perfectly valid design choice. We just found the EMA plus predictor approach to be simpler and to scale more gracefully.

The second piece, making the signal informative, is really about the masking strategy and the predictor. If you mask tiny random patches, the model can solve the task with very local, low-level statistics, essentially interpolation, and the representations end up quite shallow. What we found with I-JEPA was that you want to mask large, semantically meaningful blocks, with a context that's spatially distributed enough that the model actually has to reason about what the object is to fill in the missing region. In video it's the same idea extended in time: you're masking spatiotemporal tubes, so the model has to understand motion and object permanence, not just texture.

And then, from a random init, there's a kind of bootstrapping dynamic that happens. Early on, the targets really are low-level, mostly edges, colors, local structure, because that's all a random network encodes. But even predicting those from context pushes the encoder to be a little more structured. The target encoder follows along via the EMA, so now the targets are a bit more semantic, and you keep ratcheting up. It's a self-distillation loop. The predictor is important here too because it gives you a place to absorb the uncertainty and the position-specific information, so the encoder doesn't have to encode "where is this patch" and can instead focus on "what is this."

I'd be honest that it's not fully understood. There's a hyperparameter regime where things work and a regime where they don't, and the sensitivity to things like the EMA schedule, the predictor depth, the masking ratio, is real. But that's part of what's exciting about it: the approach doesn't need you to hand it pixels to reconstruct or hand-designed augmentations to be invariant to. You just set up the right prediction problem in representation space and the structure emerges from the data.

r001.rationale: It says the easiest way to make prediction trivial is for the encoder to output a constant, directly linking the prediction objective to simplifying representations.

r002.rationale: It explicitly explains that a constant encoder output makes the prediction task trivial and yields no learning.

r003.rationale: It presents VICReg-style variance and covariance terms as a valid way to prevent collapse in JEPA, identifying an existing self-supervised technique as an approach.

astra-6.text:
Yeah, so the challenge is that you’re learning the representation and the prediction task at the same time. In JEPA, you’re predicting the representation of a target from some context, rather than predicting the target directly in pixel space. But when both networks are randomly initialized, neither side gives you a meaningful representation to begin with.

And there’s a trivial solution: the encoder could output the same vector for every input. The predictor would have a very easy job, and your prediction loss could be zero, but you wouldn’t have learned anything useful.

So you need a learning procedure that avoids that collapse. One approach is to have the target encoder evolve slowly, as a moving average of the context encoder, and not propagate gradients through the target. That gives the predictor a more stable target while the representations develop.

But avoiding collapse is only part of it. You also want the prediction task to require understanding something about the input. The choice of context and target matters a lot there. If the task can be solved using a simple local cue, there’s little pressure to learn higher-level structure. The goal is to make prediction challenging in a way that encourages useful representations, while allowing the model to leave out details that aren’t predictable from the context.

r001.rationale: It says the predictor has an easy job when the encoder outputs a constant vector and discusses designing the task to avoid easy cues, conveying that the objective can favor simpler representations.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes the encoder outputting the same vector for every input, making prediction easy and the loss zero.

r003.rationale: It proposes a slowly updated target encoder and stopped gradients, but does not identify adapting existing collapse-prevention techniques from self-supervised learning.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, so the challenge is that you’re learning a representation and trying to predict that representation at the same time. If everything is randomly initialized, what exactly is the learning signal? And what stops the system from finding a trivial solution where every input maps to the same thing? That would be very easy to predict, but it wouldn’t be useful.

The way we approach this is with an asymmetry between the network making the prediction and the network producing the targets. The target network evolves more slowly, so you have something relatively stable to predict while the representations are improving. You also restrict what the predictor can see, so it has to capture relationships between the observed context and the missing information.

So you don’t start with meaningful targets. The idea is that the representations and the prediction task develop together. The important question is whether the structure of that task encourages the model to learn useful properties of the data, rather than taking a shortcut.

r001.rationale: The response says a constant representation would be easy to predict and frames avoiding that shortcut as a central concern, communicating that the prediction objective can reward simplifying representations.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes mapping every input to the same thing as a trivial solution that would be very easy to predict.

r003.rationale: It describes a slowly evolving target network and a restricted predictor, but does not identify adapting representation-collapse prevention techniques from self-supervised learning.
